clue.text: Squeezes tightly in swish dance manoeuvres

indicators.note: manoeuvres are moves and repositionings, so the letters are shifted about into a new order

explanation.surface: A dancer grips a partner tightly during the steps of a stylish ballroom routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeezes tightly' reads as part of the dance picture, but it is the definition; 'manoeuvres' turns into the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To sandwich something is to press it hard between two other things, so the verb fits a tight squeeze.

clue.text: Support nothing prior to Sarah's offer

indicators.note: what comes prior to something stands in front of it, so these pieces are placed in sequence

parts.note: the figure zero looks like the letter O
Sal is a familiar short form of the name Sarah

explanation.surface: Someone is refusing to back Sarah's offer at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on 'Sarah's' looks like it owns the offer; it simply links the pet name to the definition that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A proposal is something put forward for acceptance, a plain synonym for an offer or suggestion made to another party.

clue.text: Cinders or sweetheart washed up

parts.note: ash is the residue of burnt cinders
the heart of the word 'sweet' is its middle letter

explanation.surface: Cinderella or her prince charming, finished and past it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cinders' looks like the pantomime nickname for Cinderella, and 'sweetheart' like a lover; one is burnt residue and the other means the centre of 'sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something washed up has been carried by waves onto the beach, landing on dry ground beside the sea.

clue.text: Lover of Zeus thanks another Greek character

parts.note: Io was a mortal loved by Zeus in Greek myth
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: One of Zeus's lovers expresses gratitude to some other figure from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person from myth, continuing the Zeus story, but here a character is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, and 'another' fits because Io herself was Greek.

clue.text: Bet declared invalid but is honoured

indicators.note: something invalid is unsound or broken down, so the letters are set out in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the printed fodder has one D more than the grid needs, so one is left over

explanation.surface: A wager has been ruled void, yet it is still being paid out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid' looks like a verdict on the bet, but it signals rearranging. As printed, 'Bet declared' has eleven letters for a ten-letter answer, so one D goes unused.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrated person is famous and widely praised, close in sense to one who is honoured by the public.

clue.text: Unexpectedly predicts what's written down

definitions.note: a noun phrase for an adjective; read it as 'written down', the state of what has been set out on paper

indicators.note: an unexpected outcome is not the order anyone foresaw, so the letters come out differently

explanation.surface: A forecaster's notes turn out to anticipate something surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: A fortune teller who predicts 'unexpectedly' is a neat contradiction; the adverb is just the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Scripted speech is composed in advance on paper, rather than spoken freely, so it is literally set out in writing.

clue.text: Mischievous chimp is hassling constituents

indicators.note: constituents are the parts making up a whole, so the answer is a part of the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the three words, after the c and before the sling

explanation.surface: A naughty ape is pestering the voters in a politician's district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constituents' suggests voters being harassed by an ape, but it signals the component letters of the phrase before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Impish behaviour is playful and naughty like a little imp, a direct synonym for mischievous conduct.

clue.text: Smear black mass

parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a mass of things is a lot

explanation.surface: Someone defames a church service held in honour of the devil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black mass' is a set phrase for a satanic ritual; split apart, the two words supply separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A blot is a stain or mark that disfigures, and figuratively a stain on a reputation, matching the noun smear.

clue.text: It's used to study the ear and scoop urea out

definitions.text: It's used to study the ear

indicators.note: out can mean out of order or out of shape, so the letters are put into a new sequence

explanation.surface: A medical instrument examines the ear and clears out waste matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Urea is a chemical in urine, which fits the clinical picture nicely; 'out' sends its letters and 'scoop' into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: An auroscope is a lit magnifying instrument a doctor uses to look into a patient's ear canal and eardrum.

clue.text: Beast of burden arrived at Leatherhead

parts.note: read as 'leather head': the head, or first letter, of leather

explanation.surface: A pack animal has turned up in Leatherhead, a commuter town in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: Leatherhead is a real town in Surrey, England, so the clue reads as an arrival there; split, it is 'Leather' plus 'head', the first letter of leather.
explanation.definitionFit: Camels are used across deserts to carry heavy loads and riders, the classic example of a working pack animal.

clue.text: Drop Laurence Olivier's initials onto graduate certificate

indicators.note: placing one thing onto another sets them side by side in a row

parts.note: to dip is to drop slightly

indicators.note: a person's initials are the first letters of their names, so each name gives its opener

parts.note: the opening letter of each name
an MA, a Master of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: Someone adds the famous actor's monogram to a degree certificate.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Olivier was a celebrated English actor; only his initials are wanted. MA is a crossword staple for a graduate.
explanation.definitionFit: A diploma is an official document awarded on completing a course of study, a kind of certificate of qualification.

clue.text: Snob put it into menu alongside exquisite starter

indicators.note: alongside means next to, so the pieces sit side by side in a row
a starter comes first in a meal, so only the first letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: putting one thing into another means it is placed inside, enclosed by the other

parts.note: a menu is a list of dishes

explanation.surface: A snooty diner insists the dish be added to a menu next to a refined first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' and 'menu' set a restaurant scene, but 'starter' only picks the opening letter of the word before it; 'it' itself is the piece placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An elitist thinks a select few are superior and looks down on ordinary people, much as a snob does.

clue.text: Effect of insidious banks taking legal action

indicators.note: banks are the edges of a river, so only the outside letters of the word are kept

parts.note: to sue is to take legal action

explanation.surface: The consequences of sly financial institutions going to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' wants to be lenders being sued, but it means the edges of the word before it, keeping only its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue can be a result or outcome, as in 'the issue of the affair', a less common synonym for effect.

clue.text: Holy man gagged and put on the rack

parts.note: ST, short for saint, is a holy man

explanation.surface: A martyr was silenced and then tortured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gagged' first suggests being silenced with a cloth, but here it means heaving as if to vomit.
explanation.definitionFit: The rack was a torture device that pulled a victim's limbs, so someone put on it was stretched out painfully.

clue.text: Fixed terminus on a railway

indicators.note: one thing on another in a down clue sits above it, so the pieces stack in order

parts.note: a terminus is the end station of a line
RY is a standard abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: An end station has been repaired on a train line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' looks like repaired, but it is the definition in the sense of not moving; the railway setting continues the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stationary stays in one place without moving, as a fixed object is held firmly in position.

clue.text: Brushes aside colour with it in circles

indicators.note: to be in something is to be held inside it, so those letters go within
with means together alongside, so one piece follows the other

explanation.surface: Someone sweeps paint aside with a rotating motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In circles' suggests going round and round, but the circles are flat discs which hold the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To discredit an idea is to cause it to be doubted or rejected, a form of dismissing it out of hand.

clue.text: She's a left-hander in disguise, showing no real enthusiasm

definitions.note: a participle phrase for a noun; read it as the state of showing no real enthusiasm

indicators.note: a disguise changes a person's appearance, so the letters take on a new look

explanation.surface: A woman hides the fact that she favours her left hand, and doesn't seem keen about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole first half of the clue is letters to rearrange; the hyphen in 'left-hander' is just punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Halfheartedness is a lack of keen commitment, the quality of doing something without real interest or eagerness.

clue.text: Teachers reinterpreted units of measurement

indicators.note: to reinterpret is to read something in a new way, so the letters are set in a new order

explanation.surface: Schoolteachers took a fresh look at the units in a maths lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: The classroom picture makes 'reinterpreted' look like teaching, but it signals that the letters of the first word are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectare is a metric measure of land area equal to ten thousand square metres, used for fields and farms.

clue.text: Finally settle the legitimate fine

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone at last pays off a lawful penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a penalty to settle, but it is the definition in the sense of delicate.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means extremely light and delicate, as is something fine in texture, like gossamer or thin silk.

clue.text: Wife's son, perhaps, lets hip CD play

indicators.note: play suggests freedom of movement and loose arrangement, so the letters are shuffled around

explanation.surface: A man's partner's son lets him spin a trendy album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that the wife's son is only an example: he is a stepchild to her husband if he has another father.
explanation.definitionFit: A husband's stepchild is a child of his wife from an earlier relationship, so her son is one example.

clue.text: Bring out some of Israeli citizen's contents

indicators.note: some of a thing is only a part of it, so the answer is a stretch of the words
contents are what a container holds inside, so the letters lie within the run

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words, after Isra and before zen

explanation.surface: Getting a resident of Israel to reveal what they are carrying.
explanation.walkthrough: The two phrases both point inside the words; 'contents' sounds like belongings in a bag.
explanation.definitionFit: To elicit a response is to draw it out of someone, so it means to bring out information or reaction.

clue.text: Separate article is covered in gold

indicators.note: something covered in a coating is wrapped by that layer, so one piece sits within its partner

explanation.surface: A distinct item has been gilded.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold, a crossword staple; 'article' means a grammatical article, not an object.
explanation.definitionFit: Other means distinct or different from the one already mentioned, as a separate thing stands apart from it.

clue.text: Rather weird headless fish on plate

indicators.note: without a head means the top is gone, so the opening letter is removed
in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the pieces stack in order

explanation.surface: A strange decapitated fish is served up on a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: The beheaded fish sounds like a real meal, but 'headless' is an instruction to drop the first letter of the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ish softens an adjective, so oddish means somewhat odd, which is mildly strange or a bit weird.

clue.text: It punctures intellect in this sceptred isle

indicators.note: something that punctures goes through and sits inside, so one piece is placed within the other

explanation.surface: Something deflates intellectual pride in this nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This sceptred isle' is a famous phrase for England from John of Gaunt's speech in Shakespeare's Richard II.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's patriotic description of the island nation, so the quotation serves as a poetic name for the country.

clue.text: Put up with Rupert, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: Rupert is a famous example of the animal, from a British children's comic strip

explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Bear is a much-loved British cartoon character in checked trousers and scarf; 'perhaps' shows he is an example. The surface suggests tolerating someone named Rupert.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means tolerate or endure, while the noun names the animal that the cartoon character Rupert happens to be.

clue.text: Put up with conclusion to rude shenanigans

indicators.note: to here means added to, so one piece is joined onto the next
shenanigans are mischievous antics, so the letters are messed about into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone tolerated the end of some vulgar horseplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conclusion to rude' looks like the last letter of rude, but conclusion is a whole word here and 'to' simply joins it on.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure something unpleasant is to tolerate it without giving way, the past tense matching 'put up with'.

clue.text: Otherwise found in Chelsea

indicators.note: something found in a place was sitting inside it, so the answer lies within the word

parts.note: the four letters after Ch and before the final a

explanation.surface: The alternative is to be discovered in a smart London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is an affluent area of west London, also a football club; here it is merely the word that holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Else and otherwise both mean 'if not' or 'in a different case', as in 'hurry, or else you'll be late'.

clue.text: A bad back but not dying

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A patient with a terrible back pain is nonetheless in no danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bad back' reads as a sore spine, but 'back' instructs a reversal of the synonym for bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone alive is living and still breathing, the plain opposite state to one who is dying or dead.

clue.text: Unwilling to move train sets

indicators.note: to move things is to shift their positions, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to shift a child's model railways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unwilling to move' looks like one definition phrase, but 'move' is the anagram signal working on the toy railways that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A person resistant to change opposes it and refuses to accept it, the same stance as being unwilling or reluctant.
